document_title: Not how big. What it plugs into. Petersburg's draft rules
post_copy:
On Petersburg's downtown waterfront, the Ocean Beauty cannery has been shut since 2016. Its buyer also owns its 2-megawatt transformer.

The utility projected selling all 2 MW to a data center would cut 2028's 5 percent rate increase to 0. The Greensparc data center deal didn't finalize. The owner is still pursuing a small one.

On October 5th the Assembly unanimously told staff to draft a nine-month moratorium on data centers that make their own power or skip closed-loop cooling. Its sponsor called the off-grid diesel case "probably far-fetched." Grid-tied projects could still apply.

Swipe for the draft drawn as a switch, the cannery nameplate, the May rate math and both votes.

Petersburg's supplier also powers Wrangell and Ketchikan. Should each town decide what a data center may plug into, or should the three decide together?

#PetersburgAlaska #SoutheastAlaska #DataCenterZoning

slides.headline: Not how big. What it plugs into.
It pauses on-site power, not the grid.
slides.body: The Assembly unanimously told staff to draft a nine-month moratorium on data centers that make their own power or skip closed-loop cooling. A project on Petersburg's grid could still apply for a building permit.

slides.kicker: THE CASE THE DRAFT WOULD PAUSE
slides.headline: "Probably far-fetched."
slides.body: Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor, who proposed the moratorium, said a data center running on diesel power and bypassing the grid was "probably far-fetched."

slides.headline: A shut cannery. A 2 MW transformer.
slides.body: Andrew Mazzella bought the old Ocean Beauty cannery, closed since 2016, in 2024. He also owns its transformer. Greensparc planned a small data center on that existing service, cooled by a closed loop. The deal didn't finalize.

slides.headline: Mostly falling water
slides.body: Petersburg runs on hydropower, from its own plant and mostly from the Southeast Alaska Power Agency, which also supplies Wrangell and Ketchikan. The utility said it had surplus.

slides.kicker: THE UTILITY'S PROJECTIONS, AS REPORTED IN MAY
slides.headline: What selling 2 MW was projected to do
slides.body: The deal behind these numbers didn't finalize. The developer is still pursuing a small data center.

slides.headline: 3,829 square miles
slides.body: October's draft would cover the whole borough except Kupreanof. September's stopped about nine miles south of town.

slides.headline: Tied 3 to 3 in September. Unanimous in October.
slides.body: The Assembly split on the Planning Commission's year-long moratorium. Then it backed a nine-month draft and Jeff Meucci's Title 19 zoning changes. Both return for public hearings before taking effect.
labels: "We got to get something on the books." Bob Martin, Assembly

slides.headline: The test is the plug.
slides.body: Petersburg's utility is drafting its own rules for large power users. SEAPA also supplies Wrangell and Ketchikan. Should they write the same test?

aftercare: Post Wednesday November 4th or Thursday November 5th, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time. Tuesday to Thursday 8 to 11 a.m. is normally the strongest slot, but Tuesday November 3rd is Election Day and results will crowd feeds that morning. Drafts arrive daily, and posting cadence is your call.
Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting, with every URL as plain text so LinkedIn keeps the links.

Reply to every comment in the first 60 to 90 minutes and point each question to its slide (the switch slide 2, the far-fetched case slide 3, the cannery and transformer slide 4, the hydro supply slide 5, the rate math slide 6, the borough reach slide 7, the votes slide 8). If someone says Petersburg banned data centers, correct it plainly. The Assembly only directed staff to draft, and both measures return for public hearings before either can take effect. If someone reads the 0 percent as a promise, point to slide 6. It was a May projection for a deal that didn't finalize.

Watch KFSK and the Petersburg Pilot for the first reading or public hearing on the moratorium ordinance or the Title 19 changes, and for the utility's large power user ordinance. Any of the three is a natural follow-up.
After 48 hours, note saves and comments for the ledger.
editor_notes_for_email: The research window was widened to 21 days because the week was thin, so the deck rests on KFSK reports from October 16th, October 5th, September 28th and May 1st. Every Petersburg source is KFSK; the borough site refused automated reads, so no primary borough record backs a deck claim. Nothing is in effect. Both measures are directions to staff to draft, and each returns for public hearings. The Greensparc deal didn't finalize, and the developer is still pursuing a small data center with no partner named. The three utility figures are separate May projections and are never added together. That a grid-tied, closed-loop design sits on the open side of the draft is a reading of the direction as KFSK reported it. The transformer, switch, generator, nameplate, terrain and dock are renders, not surveys. Copy desk corrections to the storyboard: slide 3 now ends at the quoted words (the source's 'worth noting' is a banned phrase outside the quote); slide 4 says he also owns its transformer (C24), not that it came with the purchase; slide 8 says Title 19 zoning changes (C09), not a rewrite.
